Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, in his commentary on Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, points to this side of al-Suhrawardī’s Illuminationism. He says that when the author—al-Suhrawardī—came across fragments of Persian books and found them consistent with matters of mystical unveiling and direct vision, he approved of them and developed them further. This became the Illuminationist principle of light and darkness. al-Shīrāzī then says that this principle “is not like the doctrine of the unbelieving Magians, who believe in literal light and darkness as two first principles, because they are polytheists, not believers in divine unity.” See the introduction to Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, Tehran ed., p. 19. Here we can see the Islamic side of Illuminationist principles.↩︎

A detailed account of the relationship between illumination and direct vision can be found in al-Suhrawardī’s Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, Tehran ed., 1313–1316 AH, section 4, article 3. al-Suhrawardī also uses two other terms for illumination and vision: qahr, “domination,” for illumination, and maḥabba or ʿishq, “love,” for vision. For him, domination is “the process of bringing into existence,” while love is “the process of perception.” Love is movement toward the completion of a perfection, whether imagined, rational, or otherwise, and God—or the Light of Lights—is the first beloved. See Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, article 2, chapter 5. Through “love,” God orders existence upward; through “domination,” He orders it downward. All existence, al-Suhrawardī says, is contained within the domination of the Light of Lights, but in a hierarchy from top to bottom. Bodies lie under the domination of souls; souls under the luminous domination of intellects; intellects under the luminous domination of the first effect; and this last under the luminosity of the Light of Lights. See al-Suhrawardī, al-Mashāriʿ wa-l-Muṭāraḥāt, p. 464.↩︎
al-Suhrawardī says, for example: “The love that every lower light has for itself is overcome by its love for the higher light.” See Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, article 2, chapter 6.↩︎

In Hayākil al-Nūr, Egypt ed., 1957, second temple, al-Suhrawardī rejects those who “imagine that the soul is a part of Him,” meaning a part of God. He regards this as a false belief: “God does not admit division, so how could the rational soul resemble a part of Him?” There is therefore no unity of being between God and the soul. Since the soul is one link in the chain of Illuminationist existence, denying unity at one link means denying it throughout the whole chain.↩︎

As evidence, we can cite part of a passage from Ibn ʿArabī’s Shajarat al-Kawn, p. 7: “God brought beings into existence through His power over them, not because He needed them. The perfection of His wisdom lies in creation, and this was to reveal the nobility of water and clay.” This clearly treats “beings,” including water and clay, as existing with an existence different from God’s. In other words, they have an existence independent of His, even though it remains connected with Him.↩︎

There seems to be some confusion here between Plotinus’s terminology and Aristotle’s. Plotinus’s First Intellect emanates, whereas Aristotle’s First Mover does not move; it moves beings by making them long for its perfection and beauty. —Publisher.↩︎
al-Suhrawardī calls the unit of “pure light” that governs the rational soul the ispahbad, a term of Persian origin. See Abū Rayyān, Uṣūl al-Falsafa al-Ishrāqiyya, p. 177.↩︎

al-Suhrawardī uses the term “mothers” differently from the Peripatetic philosophers. For the Peripatetics, the “mothers” are the four simple first elements—the stoicheia: earth, water, air, and fire—which Ibn Sīnā calls “the four first things.” See Ibn Sīnā, al-Shifāʾ, On Generation and Corruption, Cairo ed., 1969, ed. Maḥmūd Qāsim, p. 155.↩︎

al-Suhrawardī’s claim that there are many “intellects” is a response to the theory of the “ten intellects,” first formulated in Arab-Islamic philosophy by al-Fārābī and then adopted by Ibn Sīnā. When al-Suhrawardī says that their number cannot be counted, he appeals to the Qurʾanic verse: “No one knows the hosts of your Lord except Him” (Qurʾan 74:31). For this classification, see al-Suhrawardī, al-Mashāriʿ wa-l-Muṭāraḥāt, mashraʿ 6, chapter 8.↩︎
al-Fārābī was the first to formulate the theory in Arab-Islamic philosophy, but the term “ten intellects” is Plotinian. —Publisher.

We find no mention of this “suspended world” in al-Suhrawardī’s Illuminationist metaphysical system outside Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, where he calls it the world of “suspended forms” and “suspended images.” From the passages dealing with it, we can conclude that it is a world of images lying between the world of intellectual lights and the sensible world. It is neither luminous nor dark, and it cannot be perceived by the outward senses. al-Suhrawardī claims to have discovered this world through his own experiences, which showed him that there are four worlds: dominant lights, governing lights, barriers, and suspended forms, both dark and luminous, in which the wicked suffer and the blessed experience pleasure. He describes this fourth world as immense and infinite. It seems to us that al-Suhrawardī needed to insert these “suspended forms” into his Illuminationist system as a connecting link between his two worlds, the luminous and the dark, because without this link his system could not explain the relationship between them. Yet the link itself also fails to explain its own existence or how it can combine the opposites of darkness and illumination. See Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, pp. 512–515, 518.↩︎

al-Suhrawardī does not explain how this dark “matter” came to exist. In fact, he contradicts himself. On the one hand, he treats bodies as “matter”; on the other, he says they are deprived of the honor of the highest light. But if they lack this light, then they also lack the Illuminationist principle that brings things into existence. In that case, they should not exist at all. Yet he speaks of them as existing, even if their existence is secondary and accidental in relation to essence. So where did their existence come from?↩︎

The standard example of a complete definition in Aristotelian logic is the definition of a human being as “a rational animal.” “Animal” is the genus, because it includes all animal species. “Rational” is the differentia, because it is the feature that distinguishes humans from the other things sharing the genus “animal.”↩︎

“Genus” and “species” belong to what is known as the Porphyrian Tree, a hierarchical classification. Aristotle also adds what later terminology calls the “proximate genus” and the specific difference. —Publisher.

al-Suhrawardī’s rejection of the rational path to knowledge appears most clearly in his main work on Illuminationist theory, Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq. In his other works, however, he combines the rational path used by Islamic philosophers with the Illuminationist path.↩︎

al-Suhrawardī, Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, rule 389, where he says: “...Once you understand that every light that can be pointed to by the senses is an accidental light, like the light of the sun and stars, then every pure light cannot be pointed to, does not inhere in a body, and has no direction at all.” By “pure light,” he means “spiritual” light. By saying that it “cannot be pointed to,” he means that it is not like sensible things that can normally be indicated through the senses.↩︎

Ibid., article 4, chapter 6. In al-Suhrawardī’s terminology, the ispahbad is the rational soul, meaning the human soul, while the “talisman” or “idol” is a simple natural element such as earth, water, or air.↩︎
